source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in LLMs (story analogies: answer order and paraphrase)
finding: Re-ran the Webb story-analogy set (18 stories). GPT-4 is biased by answer position and hurt by paraphrase. Humans show no position bias. This paper is the source of the 89% vs 61% figures that evidence line c15 saw only second-hand.
numbers: GPT-4 (0613), 18 stories: correct answer first 1.00 (18/18), second 0.72 (13/18), total 0.86 (31/36). Webb's original GPT-4 data: 0.89 first, 0.61 second, 0.75 total. Humans (245 after 5 excluded, 6 of 18 stories each): 0.78 in both positions (564/720). Paraphrased stories: GPT-4 0.86 to 0.72 (26/36); humans 0.78 to 0.70 (503/720).
limits: Only 2023 models (GPT-4-0613), simple zero-shot prompts, no chain of thought, no reasoning model. Only 18 stories, so the authors say the paraphrase drop may not be significant. No test of shuffling or voting. Gap 10 is only partly answered.
agent_relevance: Randomise candidate order and paraphrase the cases when the agent picks which past case to transfer from. A fixed order added 10 to 28 points of position bias on a GPT-4-class model. Re-test on current models before trusting this.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in LLMs (letter strings and digit matrices)
finding: Re-test of Webb et al. 2023 with larger human samples. GPT models fall on counterfactual letter-string and alternate-blank digit-matrix variants while humans stay stable. Symbol swaps in digit matrices did not hurt.
numbers: Letter strings, 263 humans (4 excluded), 14 problems each. Accuracy for 0/1/2/3 generalizations: humans .754/.358/.317/.260; GPT-3 .488/.333/.194/.160; GPT-3.5 .350/.175/.131/.078; GPT-4 .452/.271/.219/.195. GPT-4 scored 1.0 on successor comprehension checks. Digit matrices (301 humans, 10 problems each): original digits humans .715, GPT-3.5 .813, GPT-4 .810; alternate blank position humans .771, GPT-3.5 .480, GPT-4 .477; symbols instead of digits humans .704, GPT-3.5 .790, GPT-4 .792.
limits: Models from mid 2023 (gpt-4-0613, gpt-3.5-0613, davinci-003). Zero-shot only. The authors say results may not hold for chain of thought or reasoning models. Same lab as the short CogSci version (b16/c03), so it adds sample size, not independence.
agent_relevance: A step that depends on exact positions or counting inside the model is fragile. Move position and counting work to code.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2025) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs (PNAS Nexus 4(5):pgaf135)
finding: Peer-reviewed version of the authors' reply. On permuted-alphabet letter strings, a GPT-4 variant that could write and run code reached human-level accuracy, and GPT-4 without code stayed far lower. The model used code only to turn letters into indices, and wrote it unprompted.
numbers: Humans N=99 (interval 1) and N=97 (interval 2). Human vs GPT-4 plus code: P=0.92 (no difference). Human vs GPT-4 alone: P<2e-16. Control where the code model was told not to use code: 22.5% vs GPT-4 alone 21.7% (P=0.73). Zero-shot chain of thought beat plain GPT-4 (P=0.004) but still trailed humans (P=3e-8) and trailed code (P=4.4e-5). GPT-4 identified the interval between two letters of the synthetic alphabet 10.8% of the time. 38% of GPT-4 errors were a valid alternative rule vs 39% of human errors.
limits: Same authors as the 2023 and 2024 papers, so this is still not an outside replication (gap 9 stays open). One task family, one model family (GPT-4 with code tool). The authors note code is not a human-like route and LLMs may still rely on retrieval in other domains.
agent_relevance: Supports putting exact counting and matching in code. The model wrote the code itself, so a scaffold only has to offer the tool.

source: Camposampiero et al. (2025) Can large reasoning models do analogical reasoning under perceptual uncertainty? (I-RAVEN-X)
finding: Reasoning models beat plain LLMs on Raven-style rule tasks, but fall near chance when larger value ranges and noisy perception are combined. A neuro-symbolic solver with a learned rule step kept high accuracy.
numbers: Task accuracy, I-RAVEN to the hardest I-RAVEN-X setting: o3-mini (medium) 86.6% to 17.0%; DeepSeek R1 80.6% to 23.2%; chance 12.5%. Neuro-symbolic ARLC 98.6% to 88.0%. o3-mini at high effort reached only 31.0% on the hardest setting, at 53,596 average reasoning tokens. Without noise, task accuracy over the three settings: o3-mini medium 86.6/77.6/81.0, R1 80.6/84.0/82.8. Plain LLMs' arithmetic accuracy on the wider range was 'nearing 0%'.
limits: Raven-style symbolic matrices with arithmetic rules, not language analogies. The hybrid was trained on the task family. Only o3-mini and R1 (early 2025).
agent_relevance: A code-side symbolic step stayed robust where reasoning models collapsed once inputs were noisy. Our relation lists are noisy, so inject noise into them in the test and measure the score drop.

source: Camposampiero et al. (2025) I-RAVEN-X: cost side (reasoning tokens vs a symbolic solver)
finding: Direct accuracy-against-cost comparison of a reasoning model and a symbolic pipeline on the same analogy-style task.
numbers: Average reasoning tokens per item over the three no-noise settings: o3-mini medium 5,445 / 7,884 / 7,209; o3-mini high 9,867 / 19,041 / 19,449; DeepSeek R1 4,486 / 5,550 / 5,505. The authors report the symbolic ARLC on the accuracy-versus-inference-time Pareto frontier against o3-mini.
limits: Cost is in tokens for the reasoning models but in time for ARLC, so it is not a like-for-like token comparison. Raven task, not narrative.
agent_relevance: Partial evidence for gap 5: moving the structure step to code removes the reasoning tokens for that step. We still lack a token count for LLM relation extraction.

source: Beger et al. (2025) Distinguishing performance from competence in evaluations of humanlike abstract reasoning (ConceptARC; o3, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro)
finding: Reasoning models reach or pass human accuracy on ConceptARC with text input. A Python tool did not help text input. It helped visual input.
numbers: 480 ConceptARC tasks, pass@1. Humans 73%. o3 text: low effort 68.3, medium 77.1, low plus tools 67.9, medium plus tools 75.6. Claude Sonnet 4 text medium 60.2, with tools 55.0. Gemini 2.5 Pro text medium 66.0, with tools 60.4. o3 visual: medium 5.6, medium plus tools 29.2. Re-run of 48 cases three times: rule-label agreement 66.0 to 70.9%.
limits: ConceptARC is grid puzzles, not narratives. The tools were free-form Python, not an exact mapper. Human rules were not collected for wrong answers, and 19% of human rules were unclear.
agent_relevance: Generic Python access is not a reliable gain on abstraction tasks. Give code a specific exact job rather than assuming it helps.

source: Beger et al. (2025) rule-level analysis (right answer, wrong reason)
finding: Among correct text answers, models more often used a narrow, spurious rule than the intended abstraction. Accuracy alone overstates competence in text and understates it in visual input.
numbers: Correct outputs whose rule was correct-unintended or incorrect: o3 about 27%, Gemini about 27%, Claude about 19%, humans about 7%. Visual setting, correct-intended rules vs correct grids: o3 40.0% vs 29.2%, Claude 14.4% vs 6.9%, Gemini 23.5% vs 5.8% (gaps 10.8, 7.5, 17.7 points; paired 95% CIs [6.2, 15.5], [4.3, 10.7], [14.0, 21.4]).
limits: Rules labelled by annotators (mean agreement 84.8%, kappa 0.70). Single benchmark.
agent_relevance: Score the transferred relation, not only the final answer. A right answer from a wrong mapping would fool any test of the mapping step.

source: Weitekamp and MacLellan (2026) SMTB: fast structure-mapping with tight bounds (Advances in Cognitive Systems 13)
finding: A new structure-mapping algorithm, tested head to head with SME v4 on 5,845 domain pairs. Faster, and its mappings score higher. The authors also argue that on flat first-order representations SME loses its higher-order bias and acts like greedy merging.
numbers: SME corpus 5,845 pairs (ap-physics 1,137; geometry 873; moral decision 420; oddity 3,411; thermo 4). Total solve time: SME 70.95 s; greedy SMTB 5.97 s; SMTB with branch width 3 and depth 3 30.99 s. Width 3 depth 1 gives a 5 to 15 times speed-up. Mapping score 21.6% above SME at no paired walks and 22.6% at 10 (stated scale); abstract says about 50% better on large nested domains. Starting match hypotheses were verified identical to SME's.
quote: SME becomes equivalent to greedy merging over candidate expression pairs
limits: Authors' own benchmark and scoring (they score each mapping on both objectives). The corpus is hand-built logical domains, not LLM-written relation lists. Time is for the mapper only, without relation extraction.
agent_relevance: A plain greedy one-to-one merge over typed relations is cheap (seconds for thousands of pairs). Flat LLM-written lists will not get SME's higher-order bonus anyway, so do not count on it.

source: Yuan et al. (2023) Beneath surface similarity: LLMs make reasonable scientific analogies after structure abduction (SCAR)
finding: 400 scientific analogies from 13 fields with 1,614 concept mappings. LLMs map whole systems worse than humans, and worse than their word-analogy scores suggest. A one-to-one assignment algorithm over embedding similarities beat taking the most similar concept per item.
numbers: Word-analogy test, ChatGPT 0-shot mean 77.78. Structure-abduction (RSI) test: ChatGPT 71.69 vs humans 86.43; overlap of correct answers with E-KAR 60.47 vs humans 98.70. SCAR system accuracy, four-column average: GPT-4 65.01 and with 1-shot 68.49 (garbled table, first of each row pair), ChatGPT 57.85, humans 86.03. Chain of thought helped GPT-4 but hurt ChatGPT and InstructGPT-003. Greedy and Kuhn-Munkres assignment beat max-similarity (shown in a figure; not read numerically).
limits: Models up to GPT-4 (2023), closed. Table layout partly garbled in extraction. This replaces the unverified line c25.
agent_relevance: Supports a code-side one-to-one assignment step on LLM-proposed concept pairs. Does not show it beats an LLM alone with a better prompt.

source: Yuan et al. (2023) SCAR: instruction and domain sensitivity
finding: Results moved with instruction template and domain pair. Chain of thought with explanations beat the plain 'think step by step' prompt.
numbers: Ten instruction templates tested; average system accuracy varied across templates for InstructGPT-003, ChatGPT and GPT-4. The GPT-4 domain heat map showed considerable variation by domain pair, with lower accuracy for intra-domain pairs in literature and higher between similar fields such as biology and chemistry.
limits: Exact per-template numbers are in figures and were not read. Single paper.
agent_relevance: Wording moves results. Fix the prompt across arms and report variance over templates in any test of the mapping step.

source: Xiang et al. (2026) Grounding before generalizing: how AI differs from humans in causal transfer (OpenLock)
finding: Gave GPT-5.2, Claude 4.5 Sonnet, Gemini 3 Flash and DeepSeek V3.2 the text of the three solutions from an earlier environment with the same causal structure. Gains were small or absent for most models. Humans gained a lot.
numbers: 30 agents per model per structure. Humans: attempts 20.66 to 13.85 (t(158)=4.51, p<.001, d=0.71), +33.0%. GPT-5.2 15.77 to 17.43 (no gain). Claude 4.5 Sonnet 15.74 to 12.92. Gemini 3 Flash 9.08 to 7.33, the only model with significant transfer. DeepSeek V3.2 19.35 to 17.32 (p>.05). In the text-only baseline models matched or beat humans in efficiency (DeepSeek success 96.7% CC and 86.2% CE vs humans 65%). Adding images made most models worse.
limits: Transfer here is of an exact action sequence to a similar structure, not abstract analogy. The improvement-ratio column was garbled in extraction, so only attempt counts are given. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Showing a frontier model the solved earlier case in text does not reliably help on the new one. A transferred step needs its own check (O7).

source: Jung et al. (2026) Cross-pollination retrieval: finding transferable ideas across fields (CPR)
finding: Defines relevance by structural analogy (an object mapping plus relations that hold in both) instead of topic similarity, and builds the set from cross-topic citations judged by an LLM. Standard retrievers do badly, an LLM reranker does well.
numbers: CPR-eval: 1,300 queries in 26 fields. Best of eleven retrievers Recall@10 = 0.26. LLM reranker 0.81. Fine-tuning on CPR-train (10,573 pairs) raised Recall@10 to as high as 0.70, and the gain carried to held-out domains and to analogy and reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks.
limits: Labels come from LLM judgments of analogy and transfer, which the authors flag. Paper retrieval, not mapping inside an agent.
agent_relevance: Surface-similar retrieval misses transferable cases; a model judging structure finds them. Supports a model judge to pick the source case, then a code step to check the mapping.

source: Lee, MacLellan, Weitekamp (2026) Structure-mapping-guided self-explanation for learning mathematical procedures
finding: A simulation with no LLM: mapping the worked example onto the new problem points the search to the right values and operations first. The intended procedure came first far more often than in random search.
numbers: 70 mathematical transformations, 120 changed numeric components. Intended procedure first in 104 of 120 (86.7%) vs a median of 32 (26.7%) over 100 unguided random-order runs. 93.8% fewer value and operation combinations tested. Alternatives tested before the intended one: 34 vs 575.5 (94.1% fewer). Widening operations from five to eight raised the candidate space 61.7% but the model still returned 104 intended explanations first.
limits: Symbolic algebra with hand-built typed structures. No humans or LLMs. Compared with random order, not a stronger baseline such as an LLM proposing the procedure.
agent_relevance: A measured case of mapping gating which candidate inferences are tried first. Nearest thing to gap 7, but it orders search; it does not measure wrong-transfer rate.

source: Hodel and West (2023) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs (first-hand re-read; corrects c05)
finding: c05 was filed as 'prompt-format dependence'. The paper is a counterexample study: synthetic alphabets and larger letter intervals on Webb's letter strings. Humans stay stable, GPT-3 falls. They also criticise that Webb et al. did not show the problems were absent from training data.
numbers: Humans N=121 (UW undergraduates); GPT-3 N=50 instances. Only two of six problem types ('remove redundant letter' and 'sort') kept GPT-3 near its original and near human accuracy on the modified problems; those do not need generating a letter from the full alphabet. In comprehension checks GPT-3 stayed at least 30% of its original level on all but one task.
limits: Short response paper; GPT-3 only. The authors shared their counterexamples with the original first author before running the human data.
agent_relevance: Correct c05: the Hodel and West finding is brittleness to counterfactual alphabets. Prompt format still needs to be held fixed across arms (Lewis and Mitchell reuse this prompt).

source: Paper on concept vectors and the limits of abstraction in LLM analogical reasoning (arXiv 2503.03666; abstract page, authors not extracted)
finding: A small set of attention heads carries an invariant concept vector for verbal concepts like antonym. Concept vectors can steer output. A model can hold the right internal concept and still answer wrong. No invariant linear representation was found for more abstract concepts like previous and next.
limits: Abstract page only; full text not read. Mechanistic work on open-weight models.
agent_relevance: Not testable in a scaffold. Fits K27: the failure can be in applying a relation, not in having it.

source: Paper on emergent analogical reasoning in Transformers via functors (arXiv 2602.01992; abstract page, authors not extracted)
finding: Defines analogy as inferring correspondences between entities across categories and trains small Transformers on synthetic tasks. The ability depends strongly on training data, optimisation and model size. Two parts: aligned relational structure in embeddings, and applying a functor inside the network. The same trends appear in pretrained LLMs.
numbers: Abstract reports no numbers. Accepted as an ICML 2026 spotlight (v5, 27 May 2026).

source: ATOM (arXiv 2510.22590) adaptive temporal knowledge graph construction with LLMs: run-to-run stability of extraction (authors not extracted)
finding: Re-running the same extraction prompt gives different tuples. Stability is much worse when the input is a whole paragraph than when it is a short atomic fact. This is the closest measured proxy for how stable LLM-written relation lists are.
numbers: gpt-4.1-2025-04-14, 3 runs, 2020-COVID-NYT (1,076 articles, 4,223 atomic facts). Jaccard overlap with run 1: atomic facts 0.552 +- 0.124 (run 2) and 0.534 +- 0.12 (run 3); lead paragraphs 0.212 +- 0.181 and 0.218 +- 0.195. The paper calls the atomic-fact overlap 'high' although the figure is about 0.55.
limits: News text and timed 5-tuples, not relational structure of cases. Size of the stability sample is not stated.
agent_relevance: A relation list written from a whole case may share only about a fifth of its content between runs. Write relations from small facts, extract several times, and keep relations that appear in most runs.

finding: No study found for gap 1 (structural score from LLM-written lists predicting benefit at matched tokens), gap 5 (token cost of a structured mapping step vs side-by-side cases), gap 6 (LLM analogical encoding with a random-correct-case control), gap 7 (support-threshold gating of candidate inferences in a model), or gap 8 (preregistered or many-lab replication of Clement and Gentner 1991, Gentner and Toupin 1986, Markman and Gentner 1993).
numbers: The web search tool hit its session limit; OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar returned rate-limit errors; arXiv search worked for three queries, then returned 429. Alfieri, Nokes-Malach and Schunn (2013, meta-analysis of case comparison) and Mason and Tornatora (analogical encoding with and without instructions) were identified by DOI, but their text could not be opened (publisher 403, mirror 404).
limits: Absence here reflects a blocked and shallow search, not proof that nothing exists.
agent_relevance: Treat gaps 1, 5, 6, 7 and 8 as open and run them as our own tests.
